name: Sola Busca

etymology.notes: The only unnumbered trump in most early tarot decks; here numbered 0
etymology.origin: From Italian 'matto' meaning mad, foolish, or insane

metadata.historical_figure: The figure appears to depict a Celt or barbarian, distinct from the Roman figures on other trumps

sections.Etymology: The Fool / Madman. From Italian 'matto' meaning mad, foolish, or insane. The only unnumbered trump in most early tarot decks; here numbered 0
sections.Symbolism: beginning, innocence, spontaneity, free spirit, divine madness, the outsider
sections.Historical Figure: The figure appears to depict a Celt or barbarian, distinct from the Roman figures on other trumps
sections.Historical Context:
The Mato card of the Sola Busca tarot stands apart from the other trumps, which predominantly feature Roman historical figures. The wild-haired figure dressed in simple garments represents the archetypal outsider—the one who exists beyond the boundaries of civilized Roman society. In Renaissance Italy, the 'matto' held a complex social position: sometimes revered as touched by divine madness, other times feared as dangerous. The card's placement as zero reflects both nothing and infinite potential—the void from which all creation springs.

The imagery draws on medieval traditions of the court fool, who alone could speak truth to power without consequence. The Sola Busca's Mato carries a staff and appears mid-journey, suggesting the eternal wanderer who has renounced worldly attachments. Some scholars connect this figure to the Celtic warriors Rome encountered at the edges of empire—fierce, unpredictable, and operating by entirely different rules.

The card's symbolism speaks to beginnings that require abandoning certainty. Unlike the named Roman figures who represent specific historical lessons, Mato represents the universal human capacity for fresh starts and the courage to step into the unknown without a map.

etymology.notes: Often interpreted as 'The Popular Man' or 'The Social Man'
etymology.origin: From Greek 'pan' (all) + 'philos' (loving/friend)

metadata.historical_figure: Possibly Boccaccio's Panfilo from the Decameron, or a symbolic 'everyman' figure

sections.Etymology: All-loving / Friend of all. From Greek 'pan' (all) + 'philos' (loving/friend). Often interpreted as 'The Popular Man' or 'The Social Man'
sections.Symbolism: mastery, skill, mediation, wisdom applied, social connection, magical knowledge
sections.Historical Figure: Possibly Boccaccio's Panfilo from the Decameron, or a symbolic 'everyman' figure
sections.Historical Context:
Panfilio embodies the archetype of one who possesses both knowledge and the skill to apply it. The name's Greek etymology—'friend to all'—suggests a figure who bridges different worlds through wisdom and social grace. In Boccaccio's Decameron, Panfilo is described as one who 'repeatedly emphasizes the need to look deeper into stories,' presenting 'characters and situations which hide their true nature.'

This connection to deeper seeing aligns perfectly with the traditional Magician archetype. The Sola Busca depicts Panfilio as a figure of learning and magical knowledge—one who understands that true mastery lies not in domination but in harmonious relationship with all things. The Greek roots of the name suggest Hermetic and Neoplatonic influences prevalent in Renaissance thought.

Panfilio represents the conscious will directed skillfully. Like the Magician of later decks who stands with one hand pointing to heaven and one to earth, Panfilio embodies the principle of 'as above, so below'—the wise figure who channels higher knowledge into practical manifestation through friendship with all levels of existence.

etymology.notes: References the Roman gens Postumia
etymology.origin: From Latin 'postumus' meaning last, born after the father's death

metadata.historical_figure: Likely Aulus Postumius Albinus or another member of the Postumii family from the Roman Republic

sections.Etymology: Born after / The Posthumous One. From Latin 'postumus' meaning last, born after the father's death. References the Roman gens Postumia
sections.Symbolism: mystery, hidden knowledge, inheritance, intuition, the veil between worlds
sections.Historical Figure: Likely Aulus Postumius Albinus or another member of the Postumii family from the Roman Republic
sections.Historical Context:
The Postumii were one of the most ancient and distinguished patrician families of Rome, with members serving as consuls, dictators, and military commanders throughout the Republic. The name 'Postumus' originally meant 'last' but came to mean 'born after the father's death,' carrying connotations of hidden origins and knowledge passed through generations.

In the context of the Sola Busca, Postumio represents hidden authority and inherited wisdom—that which is received from those who came before. The figure corresponds to the High Priestess archetype, guardian of mysteries that lie between the conscious and unconscious realms. This is knowledge that cannot be spoken directly but must be intuited.

Researchers have connected Postumio to 'POSTUMIUS' mentioned in Book 5 of Paulus Orosius's 'Historiarum Adversum Paganos,' suggesting the deck's creator drew from this ancient historical compendium. The Postumii's role in Roman religion and their connection to foundational myths of Rome reinforces the card's association with secret knowledge and the transmission of sacred traditions across time.

etymology.notes: Some scholars suggest this represents Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
etymology.origin: Possibly from Latin 'lenis' (gentle, mild) or a scribal error for 'Lepidus'
etymology.literal: Possibly 'The Gentle One' or corruption of Lepidus

metadata.historical_figure: Likely Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, member of the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Mark Antony

sections.Etymology: Possibly 'The Gentle One' or corruption of Lepidus. Possibly from Latin 'lenis' (gentle, mild) or a scribal error for 'Lepidus'. Some scholars suggest this represents Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
sections.Symbolism: fertility, abundance, gentleness, nurturing, creative force, material comfort
sections.Historical Figure: Likely Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, member of the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Mark Antony
sections.Historical Context:
If Lenpio represents Lepidus, this card depicts one of the most powerful men in Roman history—a member of the triumvirate that ruled Rome after Caesar's assassination. The Aemilii Lepidi were among the oldest and most aristocratic families of Rome, known for their wealth, cultivation, and patronage of the arts.

The name 'Lepidus' itself means 'charming' or 'pleasant,' connecting to themes of grace, beauty, and abundance. Marcus Aemilius Lepidus served as Pontifex Maximus, Rome's chief priest, giving him religious authority alongside political power. His role as bridge-builder between factions reflects the nurturing, unifying energy of the Empress archetype.

The Sola Busca's third trump embodies generative power and material abundance. Whether representing Lepidus specifically or drawing on the etymological meaning of gentleness, Lenpio speaks to the creative force that brings forth life and sustains it. The connection to Book 5 of Orosius reinforces the card's grounding in historical narrative while pointing toward universal themes of fertility, nurture, and the sustaining power of nature.

etymology.notes: References the famous Roman general Gaius Marius
etymology.origin: From Latin 'Marius,' derived from Mars, the god of war

metadata.historical_figure: Gaius Marius (157-86 BCE), Roman general and statesman who reformed the Roman army

sections.Etymology: Of Mars / Martial. From Latin 'Marius,' derived from Mars, the god of war. References the famous Roman general Gaius Marius
sections.Symbolism: authority, structure, military power, reform, order through strength
sections.Historical Figure: Gaius Marius (157-86 BCE), Roman general and statesman who reformed the Roman army
sections.Historical Context:
Gaius Marius stands as one of the most consequential figures in Roman history. Rising from humble origins in Arpinum, he transformed Rome's military from a citizen militia into a professional army—a reform that would ultimately contribute to the fall of the Republic as generals gained personal loyalty from their troops.

Marius held the consulship an unprecedented seven times and was called 'the third founder of Rome' for saving the city from Germanic invasions. His rivalry with Sulla led to civil war and proscriptions that traumatized Roman society. The name 'Marius' connects to Mars, god of war, perfectly embodying the martial authority of the Emperor archetype.

In the Sola Busca, Mario represents structural power, military authority, and the establishment of order through strength. The reference to 'MARIUS' in Book 5 of Orosius's history places him within a moral narrative about the rise and fall of great men. Mario/Marius teaches that authority must be wielded wisely—his reforms strengthened Rome, but his political violence showed how power can corrupt even the greatest leaders.

etymology.notes: References the Roman gens Lutatia, specifically Quintus Lutatius Catulus
etymology.origin: From Latin 'catulus' meaning puppy or whelp

metadata.historical_figure: Quintus Lutatius Catulus (150-87 BCE), Roman consul and co-commander with Marius

sections.Etymology: Little dog / Puppy. From Latin 'catulus' meaning puppy or whelp. References the Roman gens Lutatia, specifically Quintus Lutatius Catulus
sections.Symbolism: tradition, orthodoxy, teaching, cultural transmission, loyalty to ancestors
sections.Historical Figure: Quintus Lutatius Catulus (150-87 BCE), Roman consul and co-commander with Marius
sections.Historical Context:
Quintus Lutatius Catulus served as consul alongside Gaius Marius during the desperate wars against the Cimbri and Teutones, Germanic tribes threatening Italy itself. Though Marius received most of the glory, Catulus played a crucial role in the final victory at Vercellae in 101 BCE. He was known for his literary refinement and his dedication to traditional Roman values.

Catulus represented the old aristocratic traditions of Rome—piety, learning, and adherence to ancestral customs. His conflict with the populist Marius embodied the fundamental tension in late Republican politics between innovation and tradition. The name's meaning of 'puppy' or 'young dog' may seem diminutive, but in Roman culture it suggested loyalty and the continuation of lineage.

As the fifth trump, Catulo corresponds to the Hierophant—the keeper of tradition and teacher of established wisdom. The reference to 'CATULUS' in Book 5 of Orosius connects this card to themes of cultural transmission and the sometimes violent conflicts over who defines orthodoxy. Catulo reminds us that tradition provides structure and meaning, but must be held with wisdom rather than rigid dogmatism.

etymology.notes: References Sextus Pompeius, son of Pompey the Great
etymology.origin: From Latin 'sextus' meaning sixth

metadata.historical_figure: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius (67-35 BCE), younger son of Pompey the Great

sections.Etymology: Sixth / The Sixth One. From Latin 'sextus' meaning sixth. References Sextus Pompeius, son of Pompey the Great
sections.Symbolism: choice, alliance, partnership, values alignment, love and loyalty
sections.Historical Figure: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius (67-35 BCE), younger son of Pompey the Great
sections.Historical Context:
Sextus Pompeius was the younger son of Pompey the Great, Rome's most celebrated general before Caesar. After his father's defeat and murder, Sextus became a pirate king, controlling the seas around Sicily and threatening Rome's grain supply. His story is one of loyalty, loss, and the complex choices forced upon those caught in civil war.

The name Sextus means simply 'sixth,' referring to birth order, but the historical Sextus became associated with choice and alliance—he negotiated with various factions, married and divorced for political advantage, and ultimately had to choose between continued resistance and accommodation with the Triumvirate.

Connected by researchers to 'SEXTUS' in Book 6 of Orosius, this card embodies the Lovers archetype's themes of union, choice, and the alignment of values. Sesto reminds us that our choices define us, particularly in times of crisis. The card speaks to partnerships, the harmony or discord between heart and mind, and the sometimes impossible decisions love and loyalty demand.

etymology.notes: References Deiotarus, King of Galatia
etymology.origin: Likely a corruption of 'Deiotarus' (from Gaulish meaning 'Divine Bull')

metadata.historical_figure: Deiotarus Philorhomaios (c. 105-40 BCE), King of Galatia, a client king of Rome

sections.Etymology: God-Bull / Divine Bull. Likely a corruption of 'Deiotarus' (from Gaulish meaning 'Divine Bull'). References Deiotarus, King of Galatia
sections.Symbolism: triumph, control of forces, direction, willpower, divine strength harnessed
sections.Historical Figure: Deiotarus Philorhomaios (c. 105-40 BCE), King of Galatia, a client king of Rome
sections.Historical Context:
Deiotarus was the ruler of Galatia in Asia Minor, whose name in Gaulish means 'Divine Bull.' He was one of Rome's most important client kings, providing crucial military support during the Mithridatic Wars. Cicero defended him against charges of plotting to assassinate Julius Caesar in the famous oration 'Pro Rege Deiotaro' of 44 BCE.

The 'Divine Bull' etymology connects Deiotarus to ancient fertility cults and the raw power of nature harnessed for civilization. As a client king who maintained his realm through skillful navigation between powerful Roman factions, he embodied the Chariot's themes of triumph through controlled direction of opposing forces.

Researchers have identified 'DEIOTARUS' in Book 6 of Orosius as the source for this card. Deo Tauro represents victory achieved not through brute strength alone, but through the masterful direction of powerful energies. Like a charioteer controlling spirited horses, Deiotarus maintained his kingdom through decades of Roman civil war by channeling competing forces toward his survival.

etymology.notes: The cognomen of the Claudii Nerones, most famously Emperor Nero
etymology.origin: From Sabine 'nero' meaning strong, brave, valiant

metadata.historical_figure: Emperor Nero Claudius Caesar (37-68 CE), fifth Roman Emperor

sections.Etymology: The Strong One / Brave. From Sabine 'nero' meaning strong, brave, valiant. The cognomen of the Claudii Nerones, most famously Emperor Nero
sections.Symbolism: inner strength, mastery over instincts, courage, the shadow self, warning against excess
sections.Historical Figure: Emperor Nero Claudius Caesar (37-68 CE), fifth Roman Emperor
sections.Historical Context:
Nero remains one of history's most infamous rulers—emperor of Rome from 54-68 CE, remembered for extravagance, persecution of Christians, and the legend that he 'fiddled while Rome burned.' Yet his reign also saw significant artistic patronage and administrative reforms. The truth of Nero is more complex than his dark legend suggests.

The name 'Nero' derives from a Sabine word meaning 'strong' or 'brave,' though this etymology seems grimly ironic given his reputation. According to historian Michael J. Hurst, Nero 'famously blamed the fire on Christians, and tortured them to death as entertainment, being the first ruler to initiate persecution of Christians.'

Identified with 'NERONE' in Book 4 of Orosius, this card embodies the Strength archetype—but not simple physical power. True strength, the card suggests, lies in mastering one's inner beasts. Nero failed this test catastrophically, letting his demons rule him. The card serves as a warning and an invitation: will we master our shadows or be consumed by them?

etymology.notes: May reference various Romans with cognomen Flaccus (meaning 'flabby-eared')
etymology.origin: From Latin 'falco' meaning falcon; possibly a corruption of 'Flaccus'

metadata.historical_figure: Possibly Lucius Valerius Flaccus or Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, prominent Roman statesmen

sections.Etymology: Falcon / Hawk. From Latin 'falco' meaning falcon; possibly a corruption of 'Flaccus'. May reference various Romans with cognomen Flaccus (meaning 'flabby-eared')
sections.Symbolism: wisdom, solitude, keen observation, elevated perspective, patient watching
sections.Historical Figure: Possibly Lucius Valerius Flaccus or Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, prominent Roman statesmen
sections.Historical Context:
The name Falco connects to the falcon—a bird of keen sight, solitary hunting, and patient observation from great heights. If derived from 'Flaccus,' it may reference several prominent Romans: Lucius Valerius Flaccus, who served with Marius and Sulla, or Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, ally of the Gracchi brothers in their reform movement.

The falcon's symbolism perfectly suits the Hermit archetype: the wise one who withdraws to gain perspective, seeing clearly what others miss from their lower vantage points. The bird represents the soul's capacity to rise above earthly concerns and perceive truth.

Researchers connect this card to 'FLACCUS' in Book 5 of Orosius. Whether we read the name as Falcon or as a Roman historical figure, Falco speaks to the wisdom gained through solitude and observation. The card invites withdrawal not as escape, but as the means to gain the elevated perspective necessary for true understanding. Sometimes we must separate from the crowd to see where it is going.

etymology.notes: Possibly connected to Veturius, but etymologically linked to fortune
etymology.origin: From Latin 'ventura' meaning fortune, chance, or things to come

metadata.historical_figure: Possibly Veturius from the Roman Republic, or a symbolic figure representing Fortune

sections.Etymology: Fortune / The Adventurer. From Latin 'ventura' meaning fortune, chance, or things to come. Possibly connected to Veturius, but etymologically linked to fortune
sections.Symbolism: fate, cycles, fortune, change, the turning wheel, impermanence
sections.Historical Figure: Possibly Veturius from the Roman Republic, or a symbolic figure representing Fortune
sections.Historical Context:
The name Venturio derives from 'ventura'—fortune, chance, the things that will come. This etymological connection to fortune makes the identification with the Wheel of Fortune trump explicit. The concept of Fortuna held immense importance in Roman thought: she was a goddess who could raise the humble and cast down the mighty without warning or apparent reason.

If connected to the historical Veturius (referenced in Book 5 of Orosius), the card gains additional resonance from actual events—the rise and fall of Roman fortunes during the Republic's turbulent final century.

Scholars note that 'Wheel of Fortune = X VENTURIO' creates a perfect alignment of number and meaning. The card embodies the eternal truth that nothing in worldly affairs remains fixed. Kingdoms rise and fall, fortunes reverse, and the wheel continues turning. Venturio reminds us to hold success lightly and bear failure with equanimity, knowing that the wheel will turn again. This is not fatalism but wisdom—understanding that we navigate cycles beyond our control while remaining responsible for our choices within them.

etymology.notes: Almost certainly references Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous orator
etymology.origin: From Latin 'Tullius,' an ancient Roman family name

metadata.historical_figure: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106-43 BCE), Rome's greatest orator and philosopher

sections.Etymology: Of the Tullii family. From Latin 'Tullius,' an ancient Roman family name. Almost certainly references Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous orator
sections.Symbolism: justice, eloquence, defense of truth, law, principled courage
sections.Historical Figure: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106-43 BCE), Rome's greatest orator and philosopher
sections.Historical Context:
Marcus Tullius Cicero stands as Rome's supreme master of rhetoric and one of history's most influential political philosophers. Rising from the equestrian class to the consulship, he exposed the Catiline conspiracy and was hailed as 'Father of the Fatherland.' His writings on law, duty, and the republic shaped Western political thought for millennia.

Art historians at the Brera Gallery note that 'Tulio XI has an uncertain identity,' yet the connection to Cicero seems compelling given the card's themes. Cicero embodied justice in action—he prosecuted corrupt governors, defended the innocent, and articulated principles of natural law that influenced thinkers from Aquinas to the American founders.

Some interpret XI Tulio as 'a skillful defender,' perfectly describing Cicero's role. The card corresponds to Justice—not abstract principle but active engagement with truth and fairness. Cicero was ultimately murdered for his fierce defense of the Republic against Mark Antony. Tulio reminds us that justice often demands courage and may exact a high price, but remains the foundation of civilization.

etymology.notes: References Gaius Papirius Carbo, Roman tribune and consul
etymology.origin: From Latin 'carbo' meaning coal or charcoal

metadata.historical_figure: Gaius Papirius Carbo (fl. 131-119 BCE), Roman tribune who championed popular causes then betrayed them

sections.Etymology: Coal / Charcoal. From Latin 'carbo' meaning coal or charcoal. References Gaius Papirius Carbo, Roman tribune and consul
sections.Symbolism: reversal, suspension, sacrifice, betrayal, seeing differently, transformation through surrender
sections.Historical Figure: Gaius Papirius Carbo (fl. 131-119 BCE), Roman tribune who championed popular causes then betrayed them
sections.Historical Context:
Gaius Papirius Carbo's life exemplifies the Hanged Man's themes of reversal and suspension between worlds. As tribune in 131 BCE, he championed the lex tabellaria—extending secret ballots to legislative assemblies, a victory for the common people. The card depicts 'S.P.Q.R.' on a quiver, connecting Carbone to Roman public authority.

Yet Carbo underwent a dramatic reversal. Cicero himself wrote: 'The third, on ordering laws or vetoing them, belongs to Carbo, a seditious and wicked citizen.' Carbo switched from populist to aristocrat, defending Lucius Opimius—the man who murdered his former ally Gaius Gracchus. When finally brought to trial, he reportedly poisoned himself rather than face judgment.

Carbone's life illustrates suspension between opposing principles—democracy and aristocracy, loyalty and betrayal. The Hanged Man traditionally shows a figure suspended upside-down, gaining new perspective through sacrifice. Carbone's tragedy was that his reversals served ambition rather than wisdom. The card invites us to examine what we might need to release, and whether our suspensions lead to enlightenment or self-destruction.

etymology.notes: References Cato, either the Elder (the Censor) or the Younger (of Utica)
etymology.origin: From Latin 'catus' meaning wise, shrewd, or clever

metadata.historical_figure: Likely Cato the Younger (95-46 BCE), Stoic philosopher and defender of the Roman Republic

sections.Etymology: Wise / Shrewd. From Latin 'catus' meaning wise, shrewd, or clever. References Cato, either the Elder (the Censor) or the Younger (of Utica)
sections.Symbolism: endings, transformation, release, principled choice, Stoic virtue, fate
sections.Historical Figure: Likely Cato the Younger (95-46 BCE), Stoic philosopher and defender of the Roman Republic
sections.Historical Context:
Cato the Younger embodied Stoic virtue carried to its ultimate conclusion. When Julius Caesar's victory in the civil war made the Republic's cause hopeless, Cato chose death over submission—killing himself at Utica rather than accept Caesar's pardon. His suicide became a symbol of republican liberty and Stoic principle.

The card shows a figure who has slain another, with a star representing Fate above. Scholars note that 'CATONE corresponds to Death (victim on ground stabbed with his spear; Cato of Utica). There is also a star, for Fate.' The connection to the conquest of Cyprus in 58 BCE has led some to suggest the card alludes to Venice's annexation of Cyprus in 1489.

Catone as Death represents not destruction for its own sake, but the necessary endings that precede transformation. Cato chose to end his life rather than live under tyranny—a radical statement that some things are worse than death. The card speaks to inevitable transitions, the clearing away of what has served its purpose, and the stark choices that define our character.

etymology.notes: References Bocchus I, King of Mauretania
etymology.origin: From the Moorish/Berber name Bocchus

metadata.historical_figure: Bocchus I (fl. 110-80 BCE), King of Mauretania who betrayed his son-in-law Jugurtha

sections.Etymology: Bocchus. From the Moorish/Berber name Bocchus. References Bocchus I, King of Mauretania
sections.Symbolism: balance, compromise, survival, blending opposites, difficult choices
sections.Historical Figure: Bocchus I (fl. 110-80 BCE), King of Mauretania who betrayed his son-in-law Jugurtha
sections.Historical Context:
Bocchus I ruled Mauretania (roughly modern Morocco and Algeria) during Rome's war against Jugurtha. Initially he supported his son-in-law Jugurtha against Rome, but when Roman forces under Marius and Sulla proved overwhelming, Bocchus made a fateful choice: he betrayed Jugurtha, delivering him in chains to Sulla.

The historical record describes how 'He went to the aid of Jugurtha against Marius; but when his army was slaughtered, he put Jugurtha in chains and gave her to Marius.' This betrayal ensured Bocchus's survival and even expansion of his kingdom, but at the cost of sacred bonds of kinship and alliance.

Researchers connect Bocho to 'BOCCHUS' in Book 5 of Orosius's history. The card corresponds to Temperance—the blending and balancing of opposing forces. Bocchus survived by finding equilibrium between his Numidian alliance and Roman power, though at terrible moral cost. Bocho speaks to the sometimes bitter compromises required for survival, and asks whether balance achieved through betrayal is true temperance or merely expedience.

etymology.notes: Connected to olive symbolism: peace, purification, victory
etymology.origin: From Latin 'oliva' meaning olive (tree or fruit)

metadata.historical_figure: Uncertain; possibly symbolic rather than representing a specific historical figure

sections.Etymology: Olive. From Latin 'oliva' meaning olive (tree or fruit). Connected to olive symbolism: peace, purification, victory
sections.Symbolism: purification, peace, alchemy, shadow work, liberation, natural wisdom
sections.Historical Figure: Uncertain; possibly symbolic rather than representing a specific historical figure
sections.Historical Context:
Olivo presents one of the Sola Busca's more enigmatic trumps. The name derives from 'oliva'—the olive tree, whose symbolism pervades Mediterranean civilization. The olive branch represents peace, while olive oil served sacred functions in purification, anointing, and religious ceremony. The olive wreath crowned victorious athletes and generals.

Scholars note that 'Olivo is related to oliva (olive), symbolically the oil of purification, whose branch symbolizes peace and life.' The card includes a basilisk—a mythical creature associated with alchemical processes and the creation of gold. 'OLIVO corresponds to the Sun (in sky; has basilisk, necessary ingredient for getting gold, associated with sun).'

Some interpret Olivo in conjunction with neighboring cards Metelo and Ipeo, suggesting hidden meanings: 'the "SC" banner Metelo holds can be combined with "Ipeo" to spell "Scipeo" (Scipio).'

As the fifteenth trump, Olivo occupies the position traditionally held by the Devil—representing bondage, materialism, and shadow aspects. The olive symbolism suggests purification and peace as antidotes to these darker themes. Perhaps Olivo invites us to examine what binds us and how we might find liberation through returning to what is natural and sustaining.

etymology.notes: References one of several Roman statesmen named Metellus
etymology.origin: From the Roman cognomen Metellus

metadata.historical_figure: Possibly Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus or Metellus Celer (fl. 63 BCE)

sections.Etymology: Metellus. From the Roman cognomen Metellus. References one of several Roman statesmen named Metellus
sections.Symbolism: revelation, sudden change, destruction of falsehood, divine intervention, fortitude
sections.Historical Figure: Possibly Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus or Metellus Celer (fl. 63 BCE)
sections.Historical Context:
The Caecilii Metelli were among the most powerful and prolific families of the Roman Republic, producing numerous consuls, censors, and military commanders. The specific Metellus depicted likely connects to the era of the Catiline conspiracy (63 BCE), suggested by 'initials SC on card, senatus consultum,' indicating senatorial authority.

Metellus Celer served as praetor during the Catiline conspiracy and was charged by the Senate to make arrests of the conspirators. This connection to defending the state against internal threat aligns with the Tower's themes of sudden intervention and the breaking of false structures.

Researchers note 'METELO corresponds to Fortitude (warrior with column, but many homonyms)' and connect the figure to Orosius's history. The card depicts a warrior with a column—traditional symbol of strength and support.

As the sixteenth trump, Metelo occupies the Tower position. The Tower represents sudden revelation that destroys false certainties. Metellus defending Rome against Catiline's conspiracy embodies this: the dramatic intervention that exposes hidden corruption. The card warns that structures built on lies will fall, but also promises that truth, however disruptive, ultimately liberates.

etymology.notes: May reference the famous Scipio family of Roman generals
etymology.origin: Meaning unclear; some scholars suggest reading it with 'SC' from Metelo as 'Scipeo/Scipio'

metadata.historical_figure: Possibly Scipio Africanus or another member of the illustrious Scipio family

sections.Etymology: Uncertain; possibly Scipio. Meaning unclear; some scholars suggest reading it with 'SC' from Metelo as 'Scipeo/Scipio'. May reference the famous Scipio family of Roman generals
sections.Symbolism: hope, guidance, mystery, healing, light in darkness
sections.Historical Figure: Possibly Scipio Africanus or another member of the illustrious Scipio family
sections.Historical Context:
The name Ipeo remains one of the Sola Busca's puzzles. Some scholars propose reading it in conjunction with the 'SC' banner on the previous card Metelo, forming 'Scipeo'—a variant of Scipio. The Scipiones were among Rome's most celebrated military families, including Scipio Africanus who defeated Hannibal, and Scipio Aemilianus who destroyed Carthage.

Scholars note that 'the wingless dragon on Olivo would seem to go with the dragon wings on [Sc]ipio,' suggesting visual connections between adjacent cards. The Scipio family represented Roman virtue at its highest—military genius combined with cultural refinement and political integrity.

Ipeo has been 'identified as representing the Devil card' by some, while the card's position as XVII aligns with the Star in traditional sequences. If Ipeo represents Scipio, the card embodies hope arising from darkness—as Scipio brought hope to Rome during its desperate struggle against Hannibal.

The Star represents hope, healing, and guidance after the Tower's destruction. Ipeo suggests that even in confusion and uncertainty (symbolized by the unclear name), guiding light remains visible to those who look for it.

etymology.notes: References the Roman gens Cornelia, specifically a branch called Lentuli
etymology.origin: From Latin 'lentus' meaning slow, pliant, or lingering

metadata.historical_figure: Possibly Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura, conspirator in the Catiline affair

sections.Etymology: Slow / Sluggish. From Latin 'lentus' meaning slow, pliant, or lingering. References the Roman gens Cornelia, specifically a branch called Lentuli
sections.Symbolism: illusion, the unconscious, patience, hidden things, slow revelation, dreams
sections.Historical Figure: Possibly Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura, conspirator in the Catiline affair
sections.Historical Context:
The Cornelii Lentuli were a branch of one of Rome's most ancient and distinguished families. The cognomen 'Lentulus' derives from 'lentus'—slow or pliant—possibly referring to an ancestor's deliberate manner or flexible character. The most notorious Lentulus was Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura, executed for his role in the Catiline conspiracy.

Scholars identify 'LENTULO as representing Time (later called the Hermit) - a philosopher at a writing desk with burning light.' This identification suggests contemplation and the slow work of wisdom, though other sources connect Lentulo to the Moon position.

As the eighteenth trump, Lentulo occupies the Moon's position—realm of illusion, fear, and the unconscious. The 'slow' etymology suggests the gradual process of navigating darkness, where haste leads to error. Lentulus Sura's fate (execution for conspiracy) warns of how illusions and hidden plots ultimately fail.

Lentulo invites us to acknowledge what lurks beneath conscious awareness—fears, intuitions, and shadow aspects that emerge in moonlight. The card counsels patience and careful attention when navigating uncertain terrain.

sections.Etymology: Sabine / Of the Sabines. From Latin 'Sabinus' meaning Sabine, referring to the ancient Italic people. References either a Roman with Sabine ancestry or the Sabine people themselves
sections.Symbolism: clarity, joy, vitality, heritage, simple truth, life-giving energy
sections.Historical Figure: Possibly a figure of Sabine origin, or symbolic representation of the Sabine heritage in Roman culture
sections.Historical Context:
The Sabines were an ancient Italic people whose culture deeply influenced Rome. Legend holds that Romulus's Romans abducted Sabine women to populate their new city—an act that led to war but ultimately to fusion of the two peoples. The Sabines contributed fundamental elements to Roman religion, including the cult of Quirinus.

The name 'Sabino' evokes this ancient heritage—the Sabine contribution to Roman identity. Many distinguished Roman families claimed Sabine descent, seeing it as a mark of ancient virtue and hardy character. The Sabine hills remained associated with rustic simplicity and traditional values.

As the nineteenth trump, Sabino corresponds to the Sun—source of light, life, and clear vision. The Sabine association with straightforward virtue and pastoral simplicity aligns with the Sun's symbolism of uncomplicated joy and truth openly displayed.

Sabino invites celebration of what is genuine and life-giving. After the Moon's illusions, the Sun reveals things as they truly are. The card speaks to vitality, success, and the simple pleasures that sustain us—values the Romans associated with their Sabine heritage.

sections.Etymology: Nimrod. Italian form of Nimrod, from Hebrew 'Nimrod' meaning 'rebel' or 'we will rebel'. References the biblical king and mighty hunter
sections.Symbolism: judgment, divine reckoning, hubris punished, awakening, the call to account
sections.Historical Figure: Nimrod, biblical figure described as a mighty hunter and founder of kingdoms including Babel
sections.Historical Context:
Nimrod appears in Genesis as a 'mighty hunter before the Lord' and founder of kingdoms in Mesopotamia, including Babel (Babylon), Erech, and Akkad. Medieval and Renaissance tradition blamed him for constructing the Tower of Babel—humanity's hubristic attempt to reach heaven that resulted in the confusion of languages.

In Dante's Inferno, Nimrod appears as a giant in the ninth circle, babbling incomprehensibly—a fitting punishment for one who caused linguistic chaos. Dante calls him 'Nembrot,' close to the Sola Busca's 'Nenbroto.'

Scholars note: 'On the card the personage tries to defend himself from divine wrath represented by the tongue of fire descending from above, however uselessly, as the punishment has already destroyed the haughtily built tower.' Modern interpretations give meanings of 'Tyranny' and 'Jealous rulers.'

As the twentieth trump, Nenbroto corresponds to Judgment—the divine reckoning that calls all to account. Nimrod's fall illustrates that earthly power, however great, cannot challenge divine order. The card invites self-examination: what towers of pride are we building, and what genuine calling awaits when we release them?

sections.Etymology: Nebuchadnezzar. From Akkadian 'Nabû-kudurri-uṣur' meaning 'Nabu, protect my firstborn son'. References Nebuchadnezzar II, King of Babylon
sections.Symbolism: completion, worldly power, empire, integration, humility in greatness
sections.Historical Figure: Nebuchadnezzar II (c. 634-562 BCE), King of the Neo-Babylonian Empire
sections.Historical Context:
Nebuchadnezzar II ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire at its zenith, conquering Jerusalem, destroying Solomon's Temple, and initiating the Babylonian Captivity of the Jews (586 BCE). He constructed the legendary Hanging Gardens and transformed Babylon into the ancient world's greatest city. His name became synonymous with imperial grandeur and earthly power.

In the Book of Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar's pride leads to divine punishment: he is driven mad, living like a beast until he acknowledges that 'the Most High rules the kingdom of men.' This narrative of humiliation and restoration influenced centuries of reflection on worldly power and its limits.

Scholars note that 'NABVCHODENASOR corresponds to the World card' and observe that imagery of 'Alexander the Great's flying griffin throne and orb mirror Nabuchodenasor's armillary sphere, suggesting themes of flying through history/Time.'

As the highest trump (XXI), Nabuchodenasor represents the World—completion, integration, and mastery of all realms. Yet the biblical narrative reminds us that even such mastery remains subordinate to divine order. The card celebrates achievement while counseling humility: the world may be gained, but only wisdom keeps it.

description:
The Sola Busca tarot, created circa 1491 in Ferrara, Italy, is one of the earliest complete 78-card tarot decks. This classical edition honors the original tradition of the cards with their historical imagery and names.

The Sola Busca is remarkable for being the first tarot deck to feature fully illustrated pip cards, predating the Rider-Waite-Smith deck by over 400 years. Each card depicts classical and historical figures from Roman antiquity and biblical tradition

The Major Arcana features named figures rather than the archetypal titles found in later decks. The Minor Arcana suits are Cups (Chalices), Coins (Discs), Batons (Clubs), and Swords.

Historical significance:
- First fully illustrated tarot deck
- Strong influence on later esoteric tarot traditions
- Named figures drawn from Roman history and legend\n- Arabic numerals on pip cards (unusual for the era)
- Court cards numbered 11-14 rather than titled

Source: Public domain images from Wikimedia Commons (Sola-Busca category).
